Respiratory Illness Outbreak in 2019 Slowed Dutch Renewable Energy Output

AMSTERDAM, June 12 — The Dutch renewable energy sector experienced significant disruption in the summer of 2019, when an outbreak of a respiratory illness swept through several wind and solar farm sites, causing widespread worker absenteeism and temporary project delays.

According to data from the Dutch Renewable Energy Federation (DREF), more than 600 workers across the provinces of Friesland, Flevoland, and Zeeland reported symptoms of what was later identified as a severe strain of adenovirus. The outbreak, which began in late May 2019, led to the temporary shutdown of at least eight large-scale wind and solar installations for periods ranging from one to three weeks.

"At the height of the outbreak, absentee rates at some sites reached 40 percent," said Marijke de Groot, spokesperson for DREF. "This forced operators to delay maintenance and slow construction on new projects, which inevitably impacted our output targets for the year."

The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy confirmed that the illness was not life-threatening but noted that the high fever and persistent cough associated with the virus made it impossible for affected staff to perform outdoor and technical work safely. No fatalities were reported, but several dozen workers required hospitalization for observation.

Officials from Zeewind Energie, one of the Netherlands’ leading wind power operators, described the outbreak as unprecedented. "We had to halt turbine inspections and routine maintenance for almost two weeks," said Hans Verbeek, Zeewind’s operations manager. "Our teams are used to working in challenging weather, but this was a different kind of threat."

The illness was believed to have spread rapidly due to shared accommodation and transport arrangements among contract workers, particularly at offshore wind sites. The Dutch Federation of Energy Workers (DFEW) called for improved health and safety protocols in response. "We saw firsthand how quickly an illness can impact site operations and worker wellbeing," said DFEW chair Sandra Jansen. "We have since worked with employers to improve hygiene facilities and access to medical care on-site."

The disruption contributed to a 6 percent shortfall in renewable energy generation for the second quarter of 2019, according to figures released later that year. However, by the autumn, affected sites had resumed normal operations.

"While the outbreak was a setback, it also led to positive changes in site management and worker health policies," DREF’s de Groot said. "The sector is now better prepared to handle similar events in the future."
